bib.title: Machine Learning Engineering in Action, ch. 15: Quality and acceptance testing

question: What must be built between finishing model development and release (data consistency, fallbacks, acceptance testing, interpretability) to keep an ML solution healthy in production?
contributions: Training/inference skew and feature stores as the data-consistency fix
Fallback and cold-start design for prediction failures
Three qualitative QA strategies compared: biased internal, dogfooding, SME evaluation
SHAP-based interpretability with code for plots

limits: No experiments or measured results; every number is an illustrative scenario or a code parameter.
SHAP caveat the author states: it explains the model, not reality; must be explained to the business before showing plots.
Dogfooding still carries bias: employee accounts are unrepresentative and employees are more critical of their own profile.
Full model code, Optuna tuning and companion notebook live in the book's GitHub repo (Chapter 15), not in the chapter.

Shap code uses shap.Explainer on a random forest; API details (e.g. explainer.expected_value[0], waterfall_plot with a custom object) may have dated since 2022. The validate_row assert is written with a tuple, so it never fires.
practices: Validate that inference features are available online per SLA before release; check offline/online consistency by scheduled statistical job or a feature store (15.1.1).
Define each feature once in a feature store with ACID storage, low-latency serving layer, denormalised key-value model and read-only access for consumers (15.1.2).
Run key-metric definition changes through a change-point process with all producer and consumer groups, then sync via ETL to the store (15.1.3, Fig 15.4).
Avoid team-private data silos; write data where DE and others can see it, preferably a feature store (15.1.4).
Always have a fallback for model output that violates business rules or is out of range, and test the fallback repeatedly (15.2, Fig 15.6).
Ask SMEs and prior-art owners for safe ranges, defaults and past failures before designing fallbacks (15.2.1).
Provide a cold-start default (popularity, region, SME-curated, high-inventory) that is fast, simple and relevant, and reuse it as the fallback (15.2.2).
Do not release on DS-team qualitative review; prefer SME evaluation of other real users' predictions over dogfooding over self-testing (15.3).
Use unseen-data prediction distributions and random sample review, but avoid handcrafted samples or own accounts (15.3.1).
Add XAI before it is needed; use shap summary plots for global feature impact and waterfall plots for the worst historical events (15.4).
